Add five small recurring charges to your Bilt card (streaming services, subscriptions, or small autopay bills). This ensures you hit the monthly minimum to earn points on rent without thinking about it.

If your building is in the Bilt Alliance, payments are seamless. If not, Bilt processes the payment via ACH to your landlord. Confirm the first payment clears successfully.

Link your World of Hyatt account in the Bilt app. Transfer points at a 1:1 ratio. Transfers are instant, so only move points when you have a specific redemption in mind.

Industry observers note that search Hyatt.com for award availability at your target property. Start with a Category 3-4 property for your first redemption to see the system work end-to-end before targeting aspirational stays.

In a recent development, imagine checking into a Park Hyatt — marble floors, a sommelier who remembers your name by day two, a room that costs $400 a night — and knowing you paid for it with points you earned by writing your rent check. Not by flying 100,000 miles. Not by spending on a business credit card. By paying the bill you were already going to pay anyway. That's the emotional core of this sweet spot, and it's one of the most powerful entry points into travel rewards for the ChooseFI community. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

Why rent-to-hotel is one of the most accessible travel rewards sweet spots.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee.

According to recent reports, most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock.

Once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

It has been revealed that what makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

Recent findings suggest that the transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. Chase Ultimate Rewards also transfers to Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, which means if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you have a second pipeline to the same program — an notable redundancy for maximizing this sweet spot.

For 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

In a recent development, head to biltrewards.com and apply for the Bilt Mastercard (issued by Wells Fargo). The card has no annual fee. Once approved, add the card to your Bilt app and register your rent payment. If your building is in the Bilt Alliance (a growing network of partnered properties), setup is seamless. If not, you can still pay rent through the Bilt app via ACH transfer — Bilt mails a check to your landlord on your behalf, and you still earn points.

Key setup rule: Activate rent rewards in the app before your first payment cycle.

According to recent reports, before rent points post, you need five qualifying purchases on your Bilt card that statement period. Set up small recurring charges — a streaming subscription, a coffee shop, a weekly grocery run — and you'll hit this automatically. Don't forget this step; missing it means forfeiting that month's rent points.

Sources indicate that go to world.hyatt.com and use the award availability search. Select "Use Points" and search your destination and dates. Hyatt's search indicates availability up to 395 days in advance — one of the longest windows in the hotel loyalty space. Identify your property, confirm the points price and availability, then — and only then — proceed to transfer.

Never transfer points without confirmed availability. Even though Hyatt availability is generally strong, you want to lock in what you see before moving irreversible points.

In the Bilt app, navigate to "Redeem" → "Transfer Points" and select World of Hyatt. Enter the exact number of points you need. The transfer is instant — points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes, not days. This is one of Bilt's most underrated features and means you can act on last-minute availability without risk.

Return to world.hyatt.com, confirm your points balance has updated, and complete your booking. You'll pay zero fuel surcharges — the points cost is the only cost. You can also call the World of Hyatt reservations line if you need help with a complex booking or want to stack a free night certificate.

If your first-choice property is sold out on points, try these tactics:.

Sources indicate that hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. A Category 7 property might cost $500-$800 per night in cash but only 30,000 points. That gap is where your 4-8 cents per point value comes from.

According to recent reports, let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

The Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

The Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

Sources indicate that now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

According to recent reports, the experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

If you hold Hyatt Globalist status, suite upgrades on award stays are available based on availability — turning a 30,000-point redemption into a $900+ suite night. That's where the CPP ceiling of 8 cents per point becomes real.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Do: Stack Hyatt's 5th Night Free Benefit.

Sources indicate that world of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Proposal longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations.

In a recent development, hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Major Sur), availability at standard rates disappears quickly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

Do: Combine With Chase Ultimate Rewards.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability.

Bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum.

It has been revealed that this is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value.

Category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards.

In a recent development, hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

In a recent development, this redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

In a recent development, this isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

Sources indicate that this redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

No. Bilt works with any landlord that accepts payment. If your building is not in the Bilt Alliance, Bilt processes the payment via ACH. The only difference is Alliance buildings may offer additional perks like bonus points or rent credits.

It has been revealed that you will still pay your rent through Bilt, but you will earn zero points on that month's rent payment. The five-transaction requirement resets monthly. Set up autopay on small recurring charges to prevent this.

Yes. Bilt transfers to over a dozen airline and hotel partners including American Airlines, United, Air Canada Aeroplan, and IHG. However, Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value among hotel transfer partners.

Bilt caps rent earning at 100,000 points per month (equivalent to $100,000 in rent at 1x). For the vast majority of renters, this cap is irrelevant. There is no annual cap on total points earned.

Sources indicate that this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Bilt-to-Hyatt pipeline is the most accessible travel rewards sweet spot available today. You are already paying rent. The Bilt card has no annual fee. Hyatt points deliver 2-8 cents in value. The transfer is instant. If you rent and you are not earning Hyatt points from that rent payment, you are leaving hundreds of dollars in annual hotel value on the table. Start with one Category 3-4 weekend stay to see it work, then scale up to aspirational properties as your balance grows.

#45590. How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1999 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.
  • I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.
  • Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: FinisherPix Powered by Outside).

Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making plans.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

Sources indicate that this story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

Recent findings suggest that as a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

In a recent development, I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

Industry observers note that I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

Recent findings suggest that for three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

When I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

Sources indicate that I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

It has been revealed that my mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

After the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Industry observers note that this was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

Then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the aims I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

The next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

In a recent development, what I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

According to recent reports, I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

Most importantly, I still wanted to run.

I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

Sources indicate that I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

Industry observers note that they gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

Sources indicate that I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

Recent findings suggest that my younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

According to recent reports, the day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

It has been revealed that on June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

The race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

In a recent development, by the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

Recent findings suggest that I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

In a recent development, my training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

My cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

According to recent reports, I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making plans; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

According to recent reports, some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

Sources indicate that the trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

Sources indicate that honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.

Most of all: Are the benefits worth the trade-offs?

Dragon Pose Is the Essential Recovery Stretch For Tight Hips and Back

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (293 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension.
  • Sources indicate that the low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion.
  • Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension. Because cycling involves repetitive hip flexion at the top of the pedal stroke, the primary hip flexor muscle (psoas major) can tighten and become compressed over time, making it harder to access a powerful position off the bike.

Sources indicate that the low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion. In the aero position, the hip flexors, which not only flex the hip but also stabilize the pelvis and lower back, repeatedly contract without fully extending, shortening the muscles and potentially leading to low back pain and stiffness.

Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter. It can also help you during the warmer months by restoring hip extension and preparing you for the longer stride that running off the bike demands. On the run, you repeatedly load one leg as the hip extends behind the body. Dragon Pose simulates that position, so you step off the bike feeling ready to hit your running stride.

Add Dragon Pose to your recovery routine. Practice this pose after a training ride or race to stretch the hip flexors and improve hip mobility.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that multiple bike fit factors affect hip angle and comfort. This guide provides five elements of a proper bike fit for smoother pedaling and to keep your position within your comfortable hip flexion range.

Improving hip extension can help you feel less compressed on the bike, move more easily through transitions, and ease low-back discomfort.

Over a Tenth of Your Clients Are Dealing With IBS—And Here’s How to Help

📅 18 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is according to the results of a study of nearly 2,000 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).1.
  • In other research, people with IBS said they would take a medicine that carried a one percent risk of sudden death if it would cure their symptoms2—which can include urgent bouts of diarrhea, gas, or persistent constipation.
  • Industry observers note that some people with IBS experience bouts of abdominal pain they describe as worse than childbirth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is according to the results of a study of nearly 2,000 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).1.

In other research, people with IBS said they would take a medicine that carried a one percent risk of sudden death if it would cure their symptoms2—which can include urgent bouts of diarrhea, gas, or persistent constipation.

Industry observers note that some people with IBS experience bouts of abdominal pain they describe as worse than childbirth. These flare-ups can siphon concentration, interrupt sleep, and destroy work productivity.3.

As a result, many people with IBS proposal their lives around the availability of private, clean bathrooms. Fear of a sudden flare-up leads some to avoid restaurants, get-togethers, even exercising in public.

This pervading worry has a name—gastrointestinal-specific anxiety—and it can affect everything from social relationships to overall well-being. It’s also the main reason people with IBS report worse quality of life than people with other chronic conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, and end-stage kidney disease.4.

PN Super Coach Sarah Maughan, certified through Monash University—a global leader in understanding the link between food sensitivities and IBS—has witnessed how lifestyle changes can prevent flare-ups, calm GI anxiety, and allow people with IBS to live the lives they want.

“My hope is for everyone with IBS to know they have options, whether that’s turning to a physician for medication and/or a health coach to learn about lifestyle changes and how to put them into action,” says Maughan.

In this article, we’ll hear more from Maughan. You’ll also learn:.

Plus, if you’re a health coach, you’ll learn how to support clients with IBS while safely staying within your scope of practice.

Sometimes referred to as “spastic colon,” IBS is the most commonly diagnosed digestive disorder in the world, affecting about 14 percent percent of adults.5.

Unlike Crohn’s and other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), IBS doesn’t alter the architecture of the gut. When healthcare professionals use diagnostic imaging, they find no infections, inflammation, damage to the bowel wall, or other evidence of disease.

Years ago, this lack of visible disease led many healthcare professionals to assume that IBS was purely psychological. More recently, however, this thinking has shifted.

Experts now view IBS as a functional neuro-gastrointestinal disorder.

That means the nerves between the GI tract and the brain don’t function optimally, causing the brain to deliver unnecessary pain signals and interfere with typical bowel function.

IBS symptoms can come and go, with some people experiencing months or years of relief only to suffer a severe flare-up that can last hours to weeks.

In addition, not everyone with IBS experiences the same set of symptoms, which can make the condition challenging to diagnose.

The below illustration indicates the range of IBS symptoms.

Researchers are still trying to understand why the gut functions differently in people with IBS. However, they do have a few theories.

According to one hypothesis, the nerve endings in the GI tract may be overly sensitive in people with IBS. This can lead to two different sets of symptoms.

According to recent reports, ▶ Hypersensitive nerves communicate pain signals to the brain, causing people with IBS to notice digestive processes that other people wouldn’t feel. Tiny gas bubbles may be severely uncomfortable for someone with IBS, for example, but not bother someone without the disorder.

▶ Overreactive nerves can trigger GI muscles to contract with too much force, leading to gas, bloating, and diarrhea. If they underreact, the same muscles don’t contract forcefully enough, which slows the passage of food through the intestine and leads to constipation.

Another theory blames disturbances on the gut microbiome, which helps to explain why some people develop IBS symptoms after first having a severe GI illness like the Norovirus.

If you or your client suspect IBS, see a credentialed health professional.

It has been revealed that the symptoms of IBS overlap with several other gastrointestinal diseases and health conditions that can require medication, surgery, or medically-supervised lifestyle changes. These include infections, inflammatory bowel diseases, celiac disease, cancer, and food allergies, among others.

It’s especially notable to see a medical professional if you or your client notice any of the following:.

It has been revealed that in addition to ruling out other GI conditions, a healthcare professional will also ask detailed questions about you or your client’s symptoms. This information allows them to pinpoint which IBS “type” you or your client might have:.

You or your client’s IBS type will inform what your healthcare professional recommends.

According to recent reports, A healthcare provider might suggest a short course of antibiotics and antidiarrheal medicine for IBS-D. On the other hand, for IBS-C, they might recommend a fiber supplement, non-habit-forming laxative, laxative-like medication, or other medicine that reduces the perception of pain and regulates bowel movements.

In order to get the most out of the visit, you can help your client (or yourself) prepare for a healthcare appointment.

A healthcare professional will likely ask the following questions, so consider the responses beforehand:.

Another way to prepare for your first appointment?

Well, you might not like it, but it’s a good idea to….

Consider keeping a poo diary for a couple of weeks before your appointment.

According to recent reports, in the diary, track the frequency of bowel movements and other symptoms. Use the Bristol Stool Chart (below) to take note of the quality of your poo. This information can help your healthcare professional assess whether you have IBS and which type.

(To learn more about the clues your poos can hide, read: 6 reasons you should care about your poop health).

Industry observers note that in recent years, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved several new prescription medicines for IBS, along with a medical device that stimulates the cranial nerves behind the ear.

In addition, thousands of research papers have looked at the interaction between IBS and various lifestyle habits, with many promising findings.

Here are five evidence-based ways to reduce the symptoms of IBS (and bonus, many of them are great for enhancing overall health too).

People with IBS who exercise regularly tend to experience fewer symptoms and flare-ups than people who don’t exercise.

When researchers asked people with IBS to walk moderately for an hour three times a week, study participants experienced significant relief from bloating and abdominal pain within 12 weeks.6.

How exercise soothes IBS isn’t fully understood, though.

According to other research, exercise may reduce stress and improve mental health, which, in turn, may help improve communication between the gut and the brain.7 8.

Another theory argues that exercise helps encourage the growth of health-promoting gut bacteria, which may help to break down food more efficiently and decrease inflammation.9.

Anxiety, stress, and depression all activate stress hormones like norepinephrine (noradrenaline) and cortisol, which can:.

Of course, stress doesn’t come with an on/off switch.

Simply telling yourself, “Stop getting so stressed out!” won’t likely help—and may even paradoxically lead to more stress.

That’s why Precision Nutrition-certified coaches like Maughan help clients learn to focus on what’s within their control—such as practicing self-compassion, or experimenting with nervous system regulators like yoga, breathing exercises, and gentle walking.

As the image below illustrates, clients can control how they perceive, respond to, and anticipate stressors—but not always the stressors themselves.

Either way, when clients focus more on what they can control and less on what they can’t, they often feel calmer and more capable.

(If you want to help a client figure out just what’s within their control—and what’s not—try out our free worksheet: Sphere of Control Worksheet).

(Assess your current stress load by taking our free quiz: Do you have a Stress Bod?).

PN coaches have long appreciated and advocated slower, more relaxed eating.

Yes, slow eating helps people fill up on fewer calories—but it also tends to help clients reduce or even eliminate GI woes like acid reflux, bloating, and pain.

Sources indicate that for one, slower eating often translates to more chewing. In addition to mechanically mashing food into a pulp, increased chewing also allows the mouth’s digestive enzymes to pre-digest food. As a result, the stomach and intestines have to work less hard.

Plus, eating in a relaxed setting often lowers stress hormones like norepinephrine and cortisol, making it less likely that they will intensify GI pain signals.

According to Maughan, this can be especially important for young parents, as it’s not always easy to eat undistracted and peacefully when tending to little ones.

Industry observers note that (Sounds simple, but slow eating is more challenging than people think—and a lot more impactful. Learn more: Try the slow-eating 30-day challenge.).

According to research, people with IBS experience more shallow, less restorative, and more interrupted sleep.13.

Because of poor sleep quality, many people with IBS sleep more hours overall than people without IBS—yet feel less rested.

Fatigue can then set off a vicious cycle. When people don’t sleep restfully, stress hormone levels tend to be higher, which can exacerbate gut pain.14.

Sources indicate that unrested people also tend to feel hungrier during the day. Cravings for fats and sweets also intensify, driving people to reach for the very foods more likely to trigger IBS symptoms—and wolf them down too quickly.

Stopping this cycle can be challenging.

As with stress, you can’t simply will yourself to sleep more restfully.

However, the first three strategies—exercise, stress management, and slower eating—can all help.

Some PN clients have found that consuming a smaller dinner earlier in the evening gives their bodies more time to digest before bed. Other clients tell us that a relaxing pre-bedtime routine—a few minutes of foam rolling, a guided meditation, a bath, or some journalling—tends to help.

(Find out the best practices for getting better sleep by checking out our infographic: The power of sleep).

Industry observers note that while there’s no one-size-fits-all IBS diet, experts have identified several food categories that are more likely to be problematic for many people. These include:.

Sources indicate that ▶ Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, and Polyols (FODMAPs), which are a family of carbohydrate-rich foods that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine. Even in people without IBS, these foods tend to slow digestion and attract water. When gut bacteria ferment them, they produce gas, which can stretch the intestinal wall. For most, this slowed digestion and gas isn’t especially noticeable; In people with IBS, it can lead to intense pain. High-FODMAP foods include wheat, rye, barley, onions, garlic, beans, dairy, honey, cashews, some processed meats, and many fruits and vegetables. (More about FODMAPs in the next section.).

▶ Caffeinated beverages and foods, especially coffee, which trigger the release of stress hormones, stimulate the production of stomach acid, increase muscle contractions in the colon, and irritate the lining of the intestine.15.

▶ Alcohol and spicy foods that irritate the gut.16 17.

▶ High fructose corn syrup and sugar alcohols such sorbitol and mannitol, which have been linked to gas, bloating, and diarrhea in susceptible people.18 19.

▶ Fatty, greasy foods, which can slow digestion and attract water, leading to loose stools, bloating, and gas.20 21.

If the idea of giving up all the foods and beverages on the above list has you in a cold sweat, know this….

Not everyone with IBS is sensitive to the same foods and beverages.

Recent findings suggest that “Everyone can have different triggers,” states Maughan. “That’s why it’s so important to figure out what makes your body feel good and what doesn’t.”.

Sources indicate that some people struggle with apples but are okay with berries. Others can drink green tea but not black. One person might be able to consume five to eight ounces of beer but not 12. A gluten-free diet may work great for some but not others.

Sources indicate that similarly, many people find relief by avoiding certain high-FODMAP foods. However, you may only be sensitive to some FODMAPs and not others. If so, eliminating all FODMAPs would be unnecessarily restrictive and difficult to follow consistently.

For this reason, it can be helpful to try an elimination diet to see which foods and beverages are problematic—along with the quantities you can safely tolerate, says Maughan. You’ll learn more about elimination diets in the next section.

Recent findings suggest that (Want someone to walk you through exactly how to do an elimination diet? Read: How and why to do an elimination diet.).

In our online coaching communities, we often see people asking some version of the following question:.

According to recent reports, “My client just told me that she has IBS. Am I allowed to continue to coach this person?”.

The answer: Yes, you certainly can.

Industry observers note that as we mentioned, Maughan specializes in helping people with digestive problems. Coaching someone with IBS is no different than coaching a client with any other nutritional goal, she states.

According to recent reports, “Because IBS is often largely associated with what someone eats, it’s within a coach’s wheelhouse—with some caveats,” says Maughan. “You can’t diagnose your client with the condition, and you should make it clear that you’re not prescribing a diet for them. In addition, you should encourage clients to seek care from a medical professional, especially if you suspect something other than IBS is going on.”.

To stay within your scope of practice, follow these do’s and don’ts.

It has been revealed that elimination diets do what the name suggests: They exclude certain foods for a short period—usually three weeks. Then, you slowly reintroduce specific foods and monitor your symptoms for possible reactions.

Elimination diets work a lot like a science experiment that helps you identify problematic foods.

The phrase “elimination diet” may sound scary and off-putting, as if you’ll be living for months on bland food you have to slurp through a straw.

However, there are many different types of elimination diets, with some much less restrictive than others.

This is an excellent option for people who suspect they already know which foods and beverages trigger symptoms.

It goes like this: You eliminate up to four foods for several weeks. Then, slowly reintroduce them one at a time to see if your symptoms return.

Recent findings suggest that let’s say, for example, from experience, you know you feel bad whenever you eat dairy. On the lite elimination diet, you’d eliminate just dairy for three weeks. Then you’d reintroduce it to see how you feel.

If you’re unsure of how food interacts with your GI tract—but aren’t ready for a super restrictive eating plan, our Precision Nutrition elimination diet is likely the way to go.

Created by PN and approved by several registered dietitians, the plan removes many of the foods most likely to cause problems, while still including a variety of vegetables, fruits, starches, legumes, nuts, seeds, and meats, so you can continue to eat a well-balanced diet.

To learn more, download our FREE Ultimate Guide to Elimination Diets. This ebook has everything you need to be successful, including an at-a-glance chart that helps you easily follow the diet, along with recipes, meal ideas, and tip sheets.

Over several years, researchers at Monash University in Australia have developed and extensively studied a low-FODMAP elimination diet for people with IBS.22.

Unlike other types of elimination diets, the FODMAP diet is a highly specialized form of medical nutrition therapy. The FODMAP diet’s list of problematic foods (shown below) is anything but intuitive, and the reintroduction phase is more complex than other elimination diets.

As a result, if you’ve been diagnosed with IBS and suspect you have a FODMAP matter, seek the expertise of a FODMAP-certified practitioner. You can also download Monash University’s FODMAP Diet app, which will help you navigate low-FODMAP eating.

In isolation, more knowledge doesn’t always lead to more power.

For example, there’s a difference between knowing that dairy messes with your gut and doing something with that knowledge.

Similarly, you might know that you feel better when you eat a small dinner earlier in the evening, but you may struggle to initiative your life so an early dinner happens regularly.

This is where a certified health coach can help.

“Many of my clients already have an idea of the foods that tend to cause them problems,” says Maughan, “But they’re nervous to know for sure because they fear that the knowledge will make eating more challenging.”.

That’s why Maughan assures clients….

Even if you do an elimination diet and you learn your favorite food is contributing to your IBS, you don’t have to do anything with that information.

You can choose to continue to eat your favourite foods if you want, AND you can choose to avoid them when it’s really notable for you not to experience IBS symptoms, she notes.

“With knowledge, you have choices,” says Maughan.

However, ahead of Kona, Ditlev mentioned he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

Sources indicate that ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

By the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Recent findings suggest that off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

Ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.

Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

📅 20 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdfitness

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.
  • You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.
  • Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

According to recent reports, A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:.

That hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

Your body doesn’t have a cutoff age.

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

Industry observers note that as a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

Industry observers note that that’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.).

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:.

Industry observers note that is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

Recent findings suggest that but the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

You’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Industry observers note that try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!).

Recent findings suggest that grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a new skill.

2) It takes way less than you think.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

You can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down.

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

If you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Recent findings suggest that becky, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, is someone I immediately thought of when I read that initial email. She’s 77, and didn’t start going to the gym until she was 57. Here’s what she had to say:.

Sources indicate that I couldn’t have mentioned it any better myself, Becky. 😊.

According to recent reports, no matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪.

Whenever you’re ready, here are more ways we can help.

1) Here’s an article with a bunch of different bodyweight exercises and progressions you can do at home.
