Lean back as you lift your right leg so your shin is about parallel to the mat in Archer Pose (Akarna Dhanurasana). Think of drawing your right foot back toward your right shoulder (similar to Happy Baby). Press your foot against your hand or the strap and, at the same time, pull your foot toward your shoulder. Stay here for a few breaths, then release and switch sides.

Sit tall with your legs straight in front of you. Bend your right leg and cross it over your left leg, stepping your right foot to the mat outside your left thigh. Bend your left leg and draw your left foot toward your right sitting bone as you lower your left knee toward the mat. Lean forward and grab your right foot with both hands or a strap. Lean back and lift your right leg in front of you, playing with how much you can comfortably straighten it while keeping your chest lifted and your back straight in a variation of Heron Pose (Krounchasana). Reach your heel away from you and, at the same time, pull your foot toward you with your hands or the strap. Draw your shoulder blades toward each other. Stay here for a few breaths, then release and switch sides.

Sources indicate that stand with your feet hip-distance apart or wider and fold forward into Standing Forward Bend, bending your knees as much as you need. Slide your hands, palms facing up, underneath your feet so your fingers are pointing toward your heels in Hand to Foot Pose (Pada Hastasana). Shift your weight into your feet and, at the same time, pull upward with your hands as if you are trying to lift your feet off the mat. Draw your shoulder blades toward each other. After several breaths here, step off your hands, and slowly rise to standing.

Stand facing the short edge of the mat and grab a strap. Step your left foot back and turn your toes out slightly. Lift the ball of your right foot so your toes point toward the sky. Loop the strap around the ball of your right foot, then stand upright. Slide your hands up the strap until your hands are alongside your hips and the strap is taut. Press into the strap with the ball of your foot and, at the same time, use your arms to keep the strap back against your hips for several breaths in this Pyramid Pose (Parsvottanasana) variation. You can intensify the stretch in your front leg by folding your chest forward with a flat back, adjusting your hands so that they remain alongside your hips and your strap stays taut. Continue to pull the strap toward you for a few breaths, then return to standing upright. Release the strap and switch sides.

Stand facing the long edge of the mat and step your feet wide apart. Place your hands on your hips and lift your chest. Forward fold with a flat back, keeping your knees bent as much as you need, then hook your big toes with your index and middle fingers or place a strap underneath both feet in Wide-Legged Standing Forward Bend (Prasarita Padottanasana D). Press your feet down toward the mat and, at the same time, bend your elbows out to the sides as you pull the strap as if you were trying to lift it toward you. Draw your shoulder blades toward each other and away from your ears. After a few breaths here, release your grip, then slowly come up to standing.

Industry observers note that stand facing the short edge of the mat. Find a steady point straight in front of you at which to gaze. Press your left foot into the mat as you bend your right knee and lift your foot behind you toward your right sitting bone. Grab hold of your inner right foot with your right hand or wrap a strap around your right ankle and hold both ends in your right hand. Press your right foot behind you as you lean your chest forward into a slight backbend and reach your left arm forward in Dancer Pose (Natarajasana). Press your right foot toward the wall behind you and, at the same time, try to pull your foot forward with your right hand or strap. Stay here for several breaths, then switch sides.

Lie on your stomach with your legs straight, the tops of your feet against the mat, and your arms alongside you with your palms facing down. Lift your head and chest off the mat, keeping your gaze a few inches in front of you on the mat. Press your thighs against the mat as you bend your knees, draw your feet toward your sitting bones, and grasp your ankles with your hands or wrap a strap around them. Press your shins toward the wall behind you and, at the same time, try to pull your feet toward you with your hands or the strap as you lift yourself into Bow Pose (Dhanurasana). Stay here for several breaths, then release.

GLP-1 medications change how the body regulates appetite, weight, and energy. That means the nutrition, exercise, and recovery strategies professionals typically use may need to change, too.

For example, a client with a dramatically reduced appetite may struggle to get enough protein and essential nutrients. Someone who’s losing weight rapidly may also be losing strength or struggling to recover from workouts that used to feel manageable.

Others may experience medication-related side effects, changes in their relationship with food, or plateaus that require a different approach.

Effective GLP-1 coaching means understanding these physiological changes and knowing how to adapt your support accordingly.

It also means recognizing when a client’s needs go beyond coaching and require input from their prescriber or another healthcare professional.

Our 30 Unwritten Rules of Triathlon

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know.
  • Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules.
  • It has been revealed that however, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family).

Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

It has been revealed that however, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:.

Sources indicate that 2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

Sources indicate that 4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

Industry observers note that 6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

According to recent reports, 7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

It has been revealed that 8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

According to recent reports, 9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

Recent findings suggest that 13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

Sources indicate that 14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

In a recent development, 15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

Industry observers note that 16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”.

19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

Industry observers note that 20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

Industry observers note that 22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

In a recent development, 23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

It has been revealed that 24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes.

Recent findings suggest that 27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

Tech Report: 5 Wellness Trends We’d Like to See Go Away

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that let’s talk about wellness trends.
  • We’re all in bodies that are designed to decay, with minds that tend to run amok and emotions that can seem like that have brains of their own.
  • According to recent reports, routines that can support your physical, emotional, and mental well-being fall under the ever-growing umbrella of “wellness.” Many of these approaches include habits that support your life and health—those that truly make you feel good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that let’s talk about wellness trends. More specifically, let’s talk about our collective penchant for “optimizing” the human experience.

Being a person is not always easy. We’re all in bodies that are designed to decay, with minds that tend to run amok and emotions that can seem like that have brains of their own. It’s only natural to try to control what we can—and self-care provides what can seem like an ideal platform for the pursuit.

According to recent reports, routines that can support your physical, emotional, and mental well-being fall under the ever-growing umbrella of “wellness.” Many of these approaches include habits that support your life and health—those that truly make you feel good. Unfortunately, many wellness trends begin in a beneficial place and spiral out of control from there.

In a recent development, A growing corner of self-care tends to be overly focused on tracking, streamlining, and pushing extremes. Any wellness trends that make you feel inadequate or anxious (like the examples listed below), are the ones we’d love to fade into the background.

Take what, if anything, really works for you from the below trends and then notice when it’s time to let it go.

Recent findings suggest that the concept of “sleepmaxxing,” or maximizing the quality of your sleep, began swirling around social media a couple of years ago. Sleeping better is a trend we can get behind—but you don’t need expensive gadgets or high levels of anxiety to do it. More importantly, putting too much focus on your sleep habits has the potential to backfire, transforming a restful part of your day into a stressful one.

Industry observers note that good sleep is essential. Nicole Moshfegh, MD, clinical psychologist and author of The Book of Sleep, notes that proper (or inadequate) rest can affect your physical health and cognitive function, not to mention your mood. Sleep is meant to be restful. Relaxing. Restorative.

Your sleep routine should not be causing you additional stress. If habits like evening restorative yoga, breathwork, or less blue light after dark improve your sleep quality, maxx on! But should you find yourself agonizing over a sleep score or lying awake calculating how many minutes of rest you’re losing—both examples of orthosomnia—know that you’ve lost the plot.

Dunking your body into cold water might sound refreshing—and for some of the population, it is! Cold plunging is a Nordic tradition that boosts mental clarity and resilience (again, you are willingly submerging yourself in cold water) and is thought to reduce post-workout muscle stiffness, fatigue, and more.

Still, you may want to pause before adopting the cold plunge as your upcoming cure-all. One study suggests that using cold baths for muscle recovery may be more of a placebo effect than anything else, as parsed by writer Alex Hutchinson. And for those in female bodies, further research has shown that over time, exposure to cold water can adversely effect the reproductive system, and there is no proven boon to female muscle recovery.

Between phone apps, smart watches, and bluetooth-connected rings, it’s never been easier to know exactly what’s going on in your body, at least on a biological level.

Certain smart gadgets, like the Pulse Mindfulness Ring, can act as a little buddy, helping you breathe deeply, commit to daily meditation, and focus. And when used correctly, the Oura Ring can also be a mindful companion.

The matter isn’t the tracking devices themselves, but how they’re being used. Just as putting too much stock in sleep scores can be considered an obsessive condition (again, orthosomnia), too much preoccupation with the information provided by wearable devices is proven to negatively impact psychological well-being. For some—including those with eating or health disorders—this sort of constant tracking can serve as a trigger, increasing rigidity and anxiety around otherwise healthy habits.

In short, try taking your smart accessories off sometimes, just to see how you feel.

We live in a world where the breaking news about what’s going on in our minds and bodies—and, usually, what we’re lacking—is practically non-stop. And usually, there’s a supplement for that. According to one report, the global supplement market is projected to be worth $300 billion by 2028. So…ya.

Supplementing becomes an glitch when you’re adding to your stack before looking to your diet and other habits. Studies have shown that supplements and weight loss pills offer a perceived sense of invulnerability, ironically leading to poorer choices in nutrition and fitness habits.

Sources indicate that another more obvious concern is supplements offered with no scientific evidence to back up purported benefits. Fast-moving digital culture and lack of oversight means that brands can pretty much say whatever they want to, which is a good thing to remember before putting anything in your body.

If your supplements are thoughtfully chosen and supplementing an existing healthy lifestyle, you’re probably on the positive side of this trend.

The internet can make your life feel like a reality show. And if you make your living as an influencer, maybe it sort of is. But even with audience perception, brand deals, and showmanship at stake, your health and wellness routine can and should make you feel good.

At its core, self-care is for you. If sharing your journey feels beneficial for you and for them, go ahead. But when your wellness practices become more about the performance of tending to yourself and less about actually doing things that bring you peace and healing, you may want to reconsider your approach.

How Restorative Yoga Can Help Lessen the Effects of Stress

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past complications beginning in 1975.
  • Anthropologists tell us that our bodies have not changed much over our millions of years of being human.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past complications beginning in 1975. This article about restorative yoga for stress relief first appeared in the September-October 1995 matter of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Anthropologists tell us that our bodies have not changed much over our millions of years of being human. Our ancestors had the same anatomical and physiological characteristics as contemporary men and women who drive freeways and communicate via the information superhighway. We have an ancient body subjected to a modern problem: living with chronic stress.

Recent findings suggest that at one time, stress was a term used chiefly by physiologists who measured its effects in their laboratories. Today the term is used in common parlance. “I’m stressed out” is a familiar idiom describing how a life lived on overload affects health, sexual function and reproduction, relationships, job performance, athletic performance, and, most vital, one’s sense of self. The effects of stress have reached epidemic proportions in our lives, and stress-related diseases have become a medical specialty.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes the effects of stress present themselves during milestone life events: marriage, the birth of a child, getting a new job, or the death of a loved one. Other times it’s the little things that get us as we try to juggle the myriad responsibilities of job and family. Regardless of the trigger, stress is often accompanied by one or more negative effects—impatience, frustration, irritation, anger, muscle tension, headache, indigestion, or poor elimination. One thing is certain: The more stress we experience, the more its effects compound within us. When stress becomes chronic, it can lead to disease.

Stress begins with a physiological response to what your body-mind perceives as life-threatening. For our ancestors, this may have been defending against the aggression of a hungry animal. For modern-day humans, this may be living with the fear of losing a job in a sagging economy or the health crisis of a family member.

Sources indicate that whatever the stressor, the mind alerts the body that danger is present. In response, the adrenal glands, located above the kidneys, secrete catecholamine hormones. These adrenaline and noradrenalin hormones act upon the autonomic nervous system, as the body prepares for fight or flight. Heart rate, blood pressure, mental alertness, and muscle tension are increased. The adrenal hormones cause metabolic changes that make energy stores available to each cell and the body begins to sweat. The body also shuts down systems that are not a priority in the immediacy of the moment, including digestion, elimination, growth, repair, and reproduction.

These adaptive responses have been positive for the survival of the human race over thousands of years. For our ancestors, a stressful situation usually resolved itself promptly. They fought or they ran, and, if they survived, everything returned to normal. The hormones were used beneficially, the adrenal glands stopped producing stress hormones, and systems that were temporarily shut down resumed operation.

Recent findings suggest that to our detriment, modern men and women are often unable to resolve stress so directly, and live lives chronically stressed as a result. Still responding to the fight-or-flight response, the adrenals continue to pump stress hormones. The body does not benefit from nutrition because the digestion and elimination systems are slowed down. Even sleep is disturbed by this agitated state.

Recent findings suggest that in a chronically stressed state, quality of life, and perhaps life itself, is at risk. The body’s capacity to heal itself is compromised, either inhibiting recovery from an existing illness or injury, or creating a newly introduced one, including high blood pressure, ulcers, back pain, immune dysfunction, reproductive problems, and depression. These conditions add stress of their own, and the cycle continues.

The antidote to stress is relaxation. To relax is to rest deeply. Relaxation is a state in which there is no movement, no effort, and the brain is quiet.

In a recent development, common to all stress reduction techniques is putting the body in a comfortable position, with gentle attention directed toward the breath. Do these techniques really work? Scientists have researched the effects of relaxation and report measurable benefits, including reduction in muscle tension and improved circulation.

According to recent reports, among the first to study relaxation was Edmund Jacobson, M.D. In 1934, he wrote You Must Relax, a book about the benefits of his progressive relaxation techniques. He reported success in using his approach to treat high blood pressure, indigestion, colitis, insomnia, and what he called “nervousness.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of the foremost writers and researchers in the field of stress reduction today is Herbert Benson, M.D., who coined the phrase “relaxation response” to describe the physiological and mental responses that occur when one consciously relaxes. In The Wellness Book he defines the relaxation response as “a physiological state characterized by a slower heart rate, metabolism, rate of breathing, lower blood pressure, and slower brain wave patterns.”.

Industry observers note that david Spiegel, M.D., author of Living Beyond Limits, reports, “In medicine, we are learning that physical problems such as high blood pressure and heart disease can be influenced by psychological interventions such as relaxation training. Indeed, the Food and Drug Administration issued a report recommending these non-drug approaches as the treatment of choice for milder forms of hypertension. Mind and body are connected and must work together, and this should be a powerful asset in treating medical illness.”.

Indeed, body and mind are connected. Relatively newly introduced in medicine is the specialty called psychoneuroimmunology, another way of saying that body and mind—or psyche, nervous system, and immune system—are connected. This specialty understands that the health of the psyche is reflected in, and partly created by, the health of the body, and vice versa.

According to recent reports, among those whose scientific study supports the body-mind connection is Dean Ornish, M.D., author of Dr. Dean Ornish’s Program for Reversing Heart Disease. He studied those with atherosclerotic heart disease and concluded that daily periods of relaxation are essential in preventing further deterioration.

I often refer to restorative yoga poses as “active relaxation.” By supporting the body with props, we alternately stimulate and relax the body to move toward balance. Some poses have an overall benefit. Others target an individual part. All create specific physiological responses which are beneficial to health and can reduce the effects of stress-related disease.

Restorative poses help relieve the effects of chronic stress in several ways. First, the use of props provides a completely supportive environment for total relaxation.

Industry observers note that second, each carefully designed restorative sequence moves the spine in all directions. These movements illustrate the age-old wisdom of yoga, which teaches that well-being is enhanced by a healthy spine. Some of the restorative poses are backbends, while others are forward bends. Additional poses gently twist the column both left and right.

Industry observers note that third, a well-sequenced restorative practice also includes an inverted pose, which reverses the effects of gravity. This can be as simple as putting the legs on a bolster or pillow, but the effects are quite dramatic. Because we stand or sit most of the day, blood and lymph fluid accumulate in the lower extremities. By changing the relationship of the legs to gravity, fluids are returned to the upper body and heart function is enhanced.

Psychobiologist and yoga teacher Roger Cole, Ph.D., consultant to the University of California, San Diego, in sleep research and biological rhythms, has done preliminary research on the effects of inverted poses. He found that they dramatically alter hormone levels, thus reducing brain arousal, blood pressure, and fluid retention. He attributes these benefits to a slowing of heart rate and dilation of the blood vessels in the upper body due to reversing the effects of gravity.

According to recent reports, finally, yoga teaches that the body is permeated with energy. Prana, the masculine energy, resides above the diaphragm, moves upward, and controls respiration and heart rate. Apana, the feminine energy, resides below the diaphragm, moves downward, and controls the function of the abdominal organs. Restorative yoga balances these two aspects of energy so that the practitioner is neither overstimulated nor depleted.

In general, restorative poses are for those times when you feel weak, fatigued, or stressed from your daily activities. They are especially beneficial for the times before, during, and after major life events: the death of a loved one, change of job or residence, marriage, divorce, major holidays, and vacations. In addition, you can practice the poses when ill or recovering from illness or injury.

Latest Update: Turn Your Pool Workout Into Playtime With These Game-Inspired Exercises

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable.
  • We know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Recent findings suggest that turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable. (Photo: Challenge Family).

We know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves. Either it’s too cold outside or it’s too beautiful a day to pass up a bike ride. Or perhaps there’s a storm 100 miles away that might suddenly decide to blow right over the aquatics center. But the truth is, if your workout is interesting enough, you’ll have all the excuses you need to get yourself into the pool, not out of it.

It has been revealed that and we’re not just talking about adding in a random drill here and there. Gamifying your swim workout, whether through solo exercises or team activities, helps make a workout enticing enough that you’ll want to do it over and over again. Adding an element of play to your swim can make it more challenging, productive, and fun all at once.

Sources indicate that before we get into a handful of our favorite games and drills, we asked Sage Hopkins, head coach of Women’s Swimming & Diving at San José State University, for his tips on how to make swimming more enjoyable. With these tools in your arsenal, you might not skip your pool workouts anymore, but actually look forward to them instead.

Sources indicate that first, Hopkins stresses how crucial it is to hear laughter echoing across the pool deck. This might not be possible if you’re training alone, but if you have a training buddy who always keeps you smiling, make it a priority to meet with them more regularly. Hopkins also encourages using music to establish an upbeat atmosphere; that might look like playing a pump-up song on your way to the pool, or investing in a pair of swimming headphones to keep the tunes going lap after lap.

Once you know your purpose, Hopkins notes, it’s easier to figure out what kinds of activities will make swimming more meaningful and enjoyable. Those who enjoy the camaraderie aspect of swimming and triathlon will enjoy team games like sharks and minnows.

Sources indicate that even simple details like naming a set, Hopkins indicates, can add a thrill to swimming. If there’s a test set you’re always dreading, give it a quirky or amusing name to make it seem less intimidating. You could use the most challenging triathlon you’ve ever lined up for as inspiration (The Wales One Hundreds, for instance, or the Norseman No Breathers).

Now, without further ado, let the games begin!

Sources indicate that you don’t need any fancy clubs to play a round of swim golf — just enough glycogen in your head to add numbers. Hopkins suggests this drill for data-driven triathletes because it’s easy to keep track of your progression over time. Essentially, you add the number of strokes with the number of seconds that it takes you to complete a certain distance (such as 50 yards) to get a “score.” You’ll then repeat that distance several times within a single set, trying to keep your score as low as possible. This game helps improve your distance per stroke and ultimately conserve energy.

Sources indicate that healthy suspense invites bursts of dopamine and curiosity into your workout, and it also means that there’s no one to blame but fate for back-to-back sprint sets. Make sure to write the following rules down on a whiteboard or protected piece of paper to reduce confusion.

Start by grabbing a set of waterproof playing cards, and assign a technique to each suit; for example, spades might call for kicking, hearts for drills, diamonds for swimming, and clubs for pulling. Next, assign a distance to groups of numbers (for instance, 2s and 3s might mean 50s, while 4s and 5s might mean 100s, and so on). Keep your jacks, queens, kings, and aces in a separate pile because they’ll dictate the number of repeats (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively).

So, for example, pulling a 5 of clubs alongside a queen would require you to grab your pull buoy for 2×100. Pulling a 2 of hearts alongside an ace would mean a 5×50 drill.

Another way to bring a measure of unpredictability to your workout is to roll a single die four times to determine your next set. The first roll determines your technique (5s could require kicking), the second your effort level (perhaps 4s always mean sprints), the third your distance (1s could mean 50s), and the fourth your number of reps (anywhere from 1 to 6).

If you were on a summer swim team as a kid, chances are high you played many games of sharks and minnows. The game starts out with one “shark” who tries to tag all the other “minnows” as they swim from one side of the pool to the other. Each swimmer who gets tagged turns into a shark for the next round. You can complicate this game by instituting an underwater safety zone.

In a recent development, if you have an area of the pool to yourself, form teams, set up goals on opposite walls with pull buoys, grab a ball, and play water polo. This is an excellent way to make vertical kicking, sprinting, and treading water more exciting. It also facilitates team bonding.

Head to the deep end for this game to work on endurance as you tread water and practice vertical kicking. If the lifeguards allow it, you can play water volleyball over the flags with an inflatable beach ball. Your pool might even have a water volleyball net, and some versions float so that you can move them as required.

Hopkins recommends “call it sets,” inspired by Bob Steele, to work on pacing and fine-tuning your internal clock. Essentially, you and your training partners will swim a set of 100s, and before each repeat, each one of you will predict the time you expect to hit. Whoever is closest to their estimates wins the set.

Chase sets are a fun way for training groups with seemingly disparate ability levels to unite, says Hopkins. Slower swimmers are allowed a head start, while faster swimmers are tasked with trying to catch them. Chase sets are ideally employed for speedwork, not drills.

Casino night is extraordinarily fun for large teams and helps highlight everyone’s unique talents. First, two or three swimmers who are roughly equivalent in speed line up at the blocks. Then, the other teammates line up behind the swimmer they predict will win.

From there, you’ll use cards or dice to determine the “event” that the swimmers will be competing in (see general rules above in the solo workouts). Whoever has picked the winning swimmer gets a rest break while the rest of the team completes a penalty swim (a 50 sprint, perhaps). If you have one seemingly unbeatable swimmer on the team, you can assign them a permanent handicap.

One Bike for Everything? Our Editors Tested Hybrid Bikes for Daily Riding—These 10 Picks Are Best for Commuting, Fitness, and Light Trails

📅 23 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • When I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes.
  • Industry observers note that outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

When I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes. These bicycles are ideal for riders who say, “I need a bike that does a little of everything.” If you’re seeking versatility, a hybrid is often your best bike option. They’re a good choice for general fitness, commuting, running errands, and family rides.

Industry observers note that outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine. However, in bike-speak, hybrids are a bicycle style that combines elements of road bikes and mountain bikes. Hybrids range from lightweight, sporty bikes designed for roads and bike paths to more rugged models suitable for light off-road use.

While they’re not ideal for die-hard mountain bikers or roadies seeking speed and the highest performance, hybrids work surprisingly well for many people on real-world rides. Typically, hybrids blend the lightweight frame, fast-rolling tires, and larger gears of road bikes with flat handlebars and the upright riding position of hardtail mountain bikes. Some hybrid models also feature suspension forks similar to those used on bikes designed for more aggressive, technical trails.

It has been revealed that the Cannondale Quick 3 is our overall favorite hybrid for its fast feel and smooth ride, comfortable upright riding position, and reasonable price. These qualities make it great for latest riders who may be hesitant about incorporating regular bike riding into their routine.

The Quick 3 features a comfortable Selle Royal saddle and Ergon grips. It also has mounts for adding a rear rack (the fork lacks rack mounts, however) and fenders to keep road spray out of your eyes and off your backside. While the pricier Quick 2 features a carbon fork and 1x9 Shimano drivetrain, the Quick 3 uses a steel fork and 1x8-speed Shimano system. These differences add a little weight, but the bike still has the gear range to tackle the hills on your commute or rides.

Cannondale also offers the Quick 3 with a step-through frame. It also sells the Quick CX 3 model with a suspension fork.

BUY QUICK 3 STEP-THROUGH - $749 BUY QUICK CX 3 - $849.

It has been revealed that the CTY 1.1 (by REI’s Co-op Cycles house brand) is a capable, affordable hybrid. The CTY is a great choice for a wide range of riders—especially for budget-minded beginners and commuters. The bike has an upright riding position (versus the sporty fit of fitness-focused hybrids). This geometry, along with a comfortable memory foam saddle and gel grips, makes the CTY 1.1 more comfortable than many competitors.

Commuters will appreciate the CTY’s flat-resistant, wire-bead 40mm tires with reflective sidewalls; they let you roll over potholes, dirt, gravel, random road debris, and even the occasional curb. For all-weather stopping power, REI equips the bike with Tektro mechanical disc brakes, and the Shimano 3x8-speed drivetrain gives you enough gear range to get you most anywhere you want to go.

BUY CTY 1.1 STEP-THROUGH - $649 $519.

Sources indicate that based in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood, Brooklyn Bike Co. uses firsthand knowledge to design well-priced bikes that can withstand the rigors of NYC commutes—and the brand’s Roebling model is a great example. While the Roebling’s design is simple and understated, it’s entirely practical for commuting, fitness, and leisurely rides.

Brooklyn builds the Roebling around a double-butted cromoly frame. Although its skinny tubes look retro compared to the shaped, formed ones used on alloy-framed hybrids, the bike is lightweight (approximately 30 pounds), durable, and easy to ride. The Roebling features a 1x9-speed drivetrain with an 11-41-tooth cassette and 42T chainring. This gives you an easy gear for hills and a significant enough gear for speed on flatter parts of your ride. Unlike many similarly priced hybrids, the Roebling uses V-style rim brakes. While not as flashy as disc brakes, V-brakes are lighterweight and easier to adjust.

It has been revealed that if you’re 5’6” or shorter, also check out the Lorimer. It’s essentially the same bike as the Roebling, but in smaller sizes (and in two color options).

Want the easiest-to-maintain, rust-proof hybrid for commuting and riding around town? Then, Priority’s Eight hybrid is probably the best choice you can find. Weighing only 27 pounds, the Eight is lighter than many hybrids thanks to its aluminum frame and carbon fiber fork.

Priority originally introduced its iconic Eight commuter bike in 2016 but discontinued it after a few years. However, the New York City-based brand relaunched the model due to rider demand—and it’s a winner. The Eight features a Gates Carbon belt drive drivetrain instead of a standard chain; this system requires no lube or maintenance (other than an occasional wipe-down with a rag). For gearing to scale hills and overpasses, Priority equips the Eight with an eight-speed (hence its name) Shimano Alfine internally geared rear hub with a 307% gear range.

Industry observers note that the Eight comes in traditional and step-through style frames. For all-weather commuters, Priority also offers the Continuum Onyx. It has fenders and dynamo lights that never need charging. Plus, it uses the Enviolo CVT (continuously variable transmission) rear hub. It has the same gear range as a traditional 21-speed drivetrain.

Industry observers note that test team member Tom Messina often rides the Cannondale Quick 2 for his daily commutes and on the local rail trail. He’s ridden it through snow squalls and on beautiful fall afternoons, and he’s impressed with the bike’s performance, versatility, and overall value.

According to recent reports, “At $949, you’ll be pressed to find many better options on a commuter or introduction bike than this one, especially from a brand I trust as much as Cannondale,” he stated. Messina particularly likes the bike’s low weight, wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, and sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes. “It’s a top-tier bike for those getting back into riding after a long time off, or spinning the bike path on a sunny day.”.

Sources indicate that want a suspension fork? Cannondale also offers the Quick CX 2 for $1,099.

Recent findings suggest that most hybrids use a road-style frame with a mix of mountain bike and pavement components. Scott takes a slightly different approach with its Scale Gravel series; the result is a blend of mountain bike and gravel tech ideal for adventure riding, backpacking, and commutes in foul weather or worn-out roads.

Intended “to go the distance over any and all types of terrain,” this adventure-ready variant of Scott’s Scale XC racing hardtail features an aluminum frame and carbon fork with multiple attachment points for carrying gear. The Gravel 20 has a SRAM Eagle 70 1x12 drivetrain that provides extremely low gearing, and Shimano hydraulic disc brakes ensure strong stopping power.

While the Gravel 20 is probably way too much bike for most people’s rides, it’s a perfect option if your gravel roads and rides are more extreme than most. However, if you like the look of this bike and want a lighterweight option, Scott offers a range of Scale Gravel models—some with carbon frames and electronic shifting—from $1,700 to $5,500.

According to recent reports, this FX 2 earns high marks for its value. Its aluminum frame and fork have a look and feel of some of Trek’s more premium hybrids, without the added price. Internal cable routing keeps the frame looking clean, and like its electrified counterpart, it comes equipped with a Shimano Cues 1x9 drivetrain and Tektro hydraulic disc brakes. At just 26 pounds, it’s impressively light for a bike this capable. Keep the FX 2 as-is for a sleek, fast look, or use the rack and fender mounts for added utility.

If you want big tires for soaking up rough terrain, this isn’t the bike for you. The FX 2 rolls on 35mm tires with a max clearance of 40mm, making it better suited for smooth roads and cinder trails. But if you like a fast, efficient ride, this is a great bike at a great price.

According to recent reports, even though hybrids typically blend road and mountain bike technology and features, many hybrids are biased towards riding pavement and gravel roads rather than trails. However, Polygon’s Heist 2 leans more heavily on its mountain bike DNA.

The Heist’s frame styling closely resembles hardtail mountain bikes, and its geometry isn’t too far from XC racing hardtails from only a decade ago. With a 63mm travel SR Suntour NEX fork and 1x8 Shimano Alivio/Essa drivetrain, you can take the Heist on light-duty singletrack. (Though you might want tires knobbier than the stock WTB Riddlers if you have anything but smooth trails.).

Specialized has sold its Sirrus platform for decades, and that experience reveals in this bike’s details. This bike embodies the “I need it to do everything” ethos.

The Sirrus features sporty geometry for a fast ride feel and a rigid fork to save some weight. Specialized equips the Sirrus X 2.0 with a wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, hydraulic disc brakes, and 40mm semi-slick tires for some off-pavement use. The Sirrus frame also has mounts for racks (for commuting or touring) and fenders.

BUY SIRRUS X 2.0 STEP-THROUGH - $850.

Many “women’s hybrids” use step-through frames, or are men’s bikes in a different color. As one of cycling’s only brands focused exclusively on women riders, Liv designs its frame geometries and touchpoints (such as saddles and grips) to better fit women’s bodies.

Alight is Liv’s hybrid platform; Alight models feature flat handlebars, rigid forks, 700x38c tires, and an upright riding position. This makes the Alight comfortable and stable without compromising too much speed. You can use the Alight for fitness rides and commutes since Liv equips the bike with mounts for a rack and fenders.

The Alight Disc 2 features a 1x9 MicroShift drivetrain, with an 11-46 tooth cassette and 40T chainring. This gives the Alight a low gear for climbing hills; however, some riders may find the gearing isn’t hard enough for flat sections of road.

According to recent reports, most hybrid models are traditional human-powered bicycles. However, some brands offer hybrid-style electric bikes. These hybrids feature lightweight electric motors and rechargeable batteries to provide pedal assistance up to 20 or 28 mph, depending on local regulations.

Recent findings suggest that below are two electric-assist hybrid bikes we’ve tested and recommend. For more e-bike options, check out our in-depth Electric Bike Buyer’s Guide.

This relatively affordable seven-speed model from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat—and now even more so with hydraulic disc brakes on this revamped version. Push the throttle, and the Soltera’s brushless hub motor kicks in, assisting you more gently as you begin pedaling.

The Soltera features disc brakes, an integrated light, and turn signals. The battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (a surprising feature compared to the bolt-on vibe of many bikes in this price range), which helps the bike blend in with non-electric bikes. Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a 46-pound package.

Many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds, so a sub-40-pound e-bike is rather impressive. Unfortunately, e-bikes this light are usually rather expensive. However, Velotric’s Tempo only costs $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight. Velotric achieves this weight reduction and low cost by ditching the bulky suspension fork and using a smaller battery.

Like most hybrids, and unlike many e-bikes, the Tempo features 700c gravel tires. These tires roll quicker than 26- or 27.5-inch tires on pavement while giving the Tempo improved traction on dirt roads and gravel paths. Velotric offers the Tempo in a traditional double diamond frame and a mid-step design. Both frames are available in two colors and two sizes.

According to recent reports, since riders use hybrids in different ways, brands make various styles of these bikes to meet their needs and budgets. Some focus on lightweight and speed, while others are more rugged and can even tackle some easier mountain bike trails. There are also hybrids with features such as racks, fenders, and lights for commuting and touring, as well as some e-bike models.

Recent findings suggest that when shopping for a hybrid, I recommend first thinking about where you will ride it most often. If you will mostly ride on paved roads and bike paths, consider a hybrid that focuses on low weight and has slick tires. If you’re commuting, look for bikes with mounts for racks or fenders, and have heavy-duty tires and wheels. For gravel paths or light-duty trail riding, consider hybrid models with suspension forks and knobbier tires.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, I always remind hybrid shoppers to consider a bike’s long-term use. Look for hybrids that use common, universal-sized components and avoid those with proprietary features or gimmicks. Riders often own their hybrids for several years, sometimes decades. You’ll want to be able to service and repair the bike down the line, especially if you use it for commuting.

According to recent reports, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Fresh England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Industry News: The Best Gravel Riding Pockets in the U.S.—Including One Unexpected Sleeper Spot

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been invited on gravel rides that range from a mix of road and well-maintained rail trail to rides where I wished I had a hardtail mountain bike.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are many people I talk to who say they have the best places to ride gravel.
  • Sources indicate that the definition of gravel typically exists between well-maintained packed gravel that feels like a road to singletrack that has some gravel between the more technical bits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been invited on gravel rides that range from a mix of road and well-maintained rail trail to rides where I wished I had a hardtail mountain bike. Admittedly, I’ve been the ringleader on more than one occasion for a solidly underbiked ride that was listed as a gravel ride.

Recent findings suggest that there are many people I talk to who say they have the best places to ride gravel. Some pride themselves on challenging and chunky gravel roads, while other places have gravel rides with a 10,000-foot view. And how each rider defines gravel will be different from person to person.

Sources indicate that the definition of gravel typically exists between well-maintained packed gravel that feels like a road to singletrack that has some gravel between the more technical bits. Many areas of the country may boast one great gravel quality, but this list compiles the places that check off more than a few boxes.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, it’s clear gravel riding is here to stay, but the challenge lies in deciding where to ride first. Our list has the best gravel riding pockets in the country and can serve as your checklist for 2027. The last destination on the list is a sleeper you shouldn’t miss.

In a recent development, the Fresh York Times featured a run-down of the best spots in the U.S. for gravel biking, so you know it’s now officially mainstream. Their list included Northwest Arkansas, namely Bentonville—in the heart of the Ozark Mountains—which has become known as a gravel (and all things biking) hub. That’s thanks in large part to the Walton family. The Waltons own Walmart and run the Walton Family Foundation, which has always prioritized bikes and outdoor recreation.

If you’re in the area, there are endless ways to spend a day on a bike. According to the NYT, Chuck Campbell, an environmental manager for a wastewater recycling tech giant, has designed several epic loops that together make up the 1,200-mile Arkansas High Country Route, a mix of paved and unpaved roads that launched in 2019.

It has been revealed that colorado might be home to the unique gravel races of any state, but if you’re looking for gravel events you can likely find one in just about any state these days. Steamboat Springs introduced SBT GRVL in 2019. They’ve since grown to be one of the most inclusive events out there, with all kinds of training ride opportunities, and partnerships with inclusive cycling groups such as All Bodies on Bikes and Ride for Racial Justice.

If you’re looking for a quieter way to enjoy Colorado gravel, check out Nederland, a quaint mountain town 30 minutes outside of Boulder. There are probably more gravel roads in and around Nederland than paved, and almost all of them take you to excellent cafes and snack shops to recharge. Nederland to Gold Hill with a homemade slice of pie from the Gold Hill Store is tough to beat.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a way to escape the cold in the coming months, Arizona offers tons of gravel-friendly riding. Many of the multiuse trails around the Phoenix State Parks can be connected for some hearty loops. AZ Gravel Rides has compiled an excellent list of gravel adventures in all areas of the state.

Recent findings suggest that patagonia, Arizona, has become a not-so-secret winter escape for gravel lovers lately. Located in the Patagonia Mountains, it’s got a desert mountain feel, with plenty of climbing and lots of sandy roads with incredible views. The area is expansive, so you can ride all day without seeing anyone. According to the NYT, “a upcoming edition in the expanding “Gravel Adventure Field Guide” series focuses on routes in Patagonia and surrounding Santa Cruz County.”.

And on the East Coast, Vermont can’t be beat. Most people in Vermont will probably tell you that they prefer dirt roads to paved ones. There’s something nice about a slower pace. Seven Days VT claims that Vermont has 8,579 miles of unpaved roads, compared to 7,182 miles of paved roads.

The VTXL is a 300-mile route that stretches from Canada to Massachusetts via 90 percent dirt and gravel roads. Former WorldTour rider turned adventure/gravel pro Ted King is at the moment bikepacking the route that he’s done before in a single push. This time he’s documenting the summer’s flooding that ravaged the state. “Heartbreaking but with short memories, we want to help bring attention to just how devastating it was and continues to be as Vermont rebuilds,” he posted to social media.

Sources indicate that the gravel in Vermont is extensive, but make sure you tie in a climb up the road dubbed, “the steepest paved mile in the U.S..” Lincoln Gap may be known for having the steepest paved mile in the US, but the descent down from the climb is high quality gravel. Just a heads up—if you’re a fan of breweries, then plan for more stops than you would normally expect.

Recent findings suggest that when I think of a great area for riding gravel there are some factors that the location needs to have. Hard gravel climbs with ripping descents, some views while you catch your breath on top of the climbs, and something for everyone to ride—regardless of skill level, are a few things that top my list. Northern Pennsylvania may not be among the top areas for gravel riding for many people, but it should be.

Recent findings suggest that rail trails like the Pine Creek Rail Trail leave an option for anyone to get out on gravel in this area, but there are plenty of options for the seasoned cyclists as well. Events like Endless Mountains, Unpaved Pennsylvania, and Lu Lacka Wyco Hundo boast routes from 50 miles to 430 miles long. For context—the 115-mile route of Endless Mountains had over 12,000 feet of climbing. A large majority of the route was on gravel with very little stretches of paved country roads.

While the views from the top of the hills are beautiful its worth noting you don’t have the vistas of other locations like Colorado or Arizona. The area makes up for it’s lack of high alpine overlooks or desert landscapes with tough, punchy gravel climbs and positive vibes from the locals. Make sure this unexpected gravel honey hole ends up on your destination list for 2027. If you think I missed a spot (or have somewhere I should add for my 2027 ride list), then drop it in the comments below.

Sources indicate that micah Ling is a freelance writer who lives in the mountains of Colorado. She splits her free time between mountain biking and trail running.

According to recent reports, jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

5 Cross-Training Workouts for Seniors

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2456 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.
  • It has been revealed that A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants.
  • Recent findings suggest that this doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.

It has been revealed that A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants. Individuals in the first group were between 65 and 75 years old, and those in the second group were 85 years and older. Neither group had engaged in resistance training for at least six months. After following a 12-week strength-training program, both cohorts showed significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and physical performance.

Recent findings suggest that this doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell. Age-related sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and function, can begin in your 30s, says Robert Linkul, C.S.C.S., owner of Training The Older Adult. And it only ramps up with every passing decade. “There’s a constant battle against sarcopenia,” he tells Bicycling. “But if you resistance train your entire life, your body shouldn’t change drastically. Naturally, you’ll lose some muscle mass. There’s going to be some degeneration of performance and power output. But as long as you keep trying to maintain it, you’ll have it.”.

Recent findings suggest that julie Logue, M.P.H., senior program manager for Silver Sneakers, agrees that strength training is particularly worthwhile for seniors. “As muscular strength and endurance improves, you can perform activities of daily living with greater ease,” she indicates, noting that a regular resistance training program can also help older individuals maintain bone density, improve balance, reduce the risk of falling, and correct muscle imbalances. “Because cycling uses some parts of the body more than others, strength training is a necessary complement to promote muscle balance and reduce overuse injuries. Increasing strength can also benefit cyclists by increasing overall endurance and postural control,” she says.

Convinced but not sure where to start? With Linkul’s help, we put together five strength-training workouts you can do on cross-training days. Each one includes senior-appropriate exercises, some of which can be modified or progressed depending on your skill level and experience. For exercises that require added resistance, choose a load that’s heavy but doable; on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being your max effort, aim for between a 6 and 7.

Cyclists who are entirely upcoming to strength training want to go lighter at first. “Beginning with bodyweight movements can help build a foundation for using external resistance,” Logue indicates. She also recommends consulting a primary care provider before starting any new exercise program.

Sources indicate that like most bodyweight workouts, you can do this full-body circuit anywhere, making it a convenient option for when you’re traveling, can’t get to the gym, or just don’t feel like dealing with a bunch of equipment. You’ll work every major muscle group, including your deep core, and train functional, everyday movement patterns, like standing from a sitting position, pushing up from the floor, and maintaining balance and control while stepping backward.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a chair, box, or bench.

Industry observers note that stand in front of a chair, box, or bench with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Tap the chair with glutes. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and body forming straight line from head to feet. Drive right foot to chest. Step back to plank. Repeat on left side. Continue alternating. Do 15 reps per side.

In a recent development, stand with feet hip-width apart. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward. Repeat, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

In a recent development, start faceup with arms at sides, legs together, and feet on an elevated surface, like a small box, bench, or chair. Engage core and lift hips off ground so body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders. (Head and shoulders stay on ground, like a straight-leg glute bridge.) Allow arms to rest on ground or, for added difficulty, lift them off floor so elbows are straight and fingertips point up. Hold for 30-60 seconds.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start in plank position, shoulders over wrists and forming straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows, lowering body to floor while maintaining straight line. Press back up to plank. Repeat. Do 12 reps. Perform on knees or with hands against wall to make it easier.

This workout develops core strength through exercises that challenge your balance and train transferable skills, like carrying a heavy load, crawling in multiple directions, and shifting your body weight from a lying-down position. The single-leg glute bridge and superman variation fire up the posterior chain, which is critical for cyclists, and the three-way toe tap will help improve your overall balance and stability.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a dumbbell or kettlebell.

Start on hands and knees, shoulders over wrists and knees under hips. Lift knees just about an inch off floor. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the right. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot backward. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the left. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot forward. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps.

According to recent reports, stand with feet together. Send hips back, back flat and core engage, to lower into a shallow hinge position. Keeping weight on left leg, tap right foot forward, then back to left foot. Tap right foot out to the side, then back to left foot. Tap right foot backward, then back to left foot. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Tap right hand to left shoulder. Then return to plank. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand, stand tall with shoulders back, chin parallel to the floor, and arms straight down at sides. Keep shoulders over hips (be careful not to lean away from weighted arm) and relax shoulders as you slowly walk forward for 30-60 seconds. Repeat, holding weight on opposite side.

In a recent development, lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted, arms down by sides. Lift and straighten right leg, knees in line. Drive through left foot to lift hips up. Pause, then slowly lower back down. Lift with glutes and hamstrings, rather than low back. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

A dedicated upper-body workout counteracts the time cyclists spend leaning forward in a rounded position and can help correct postural challenges, alleviate back pain, and lead to better performance on the bike. This workout includes both pushing and pulling movement patterns and targets the muscles of the chest, back, shoulders, arms, and core.

Recent findings suggest that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, and a medicine ball.

Recent findings suggest that lie faceup on a bench or mat, knees bent and feet planted, holding a dumbbell in each hand, held above shoulders. Slowly lower weights toward chest, bending elbows, with elbows about 45 degrees from torso. Press weights back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

It has been revealed that start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg bent or straight (whatever is more comfortable). Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand, arm extended down in front of you. This is the starting position. Row weight to hip by pulling elbow back and keeping it close to side. Keep shoulders down and back, back flat, and core engaged. Extended arm back down slowly to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders with elbows bent and palms facing each other. Press weights overhead, extending arms. Slowly lower back down to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Recent findings suggest that start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg straight. Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand at hip with elbow bent. This is the starting position. Straighten right arm back behind you, extending elbow. Bend elbow to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Recent findings suggest that stand with feet shoulder-width apart in front of a wall, a little farther than arm’s length away, slight bend in knees, holding a medicine ball at chest. Toss medicine ball toward wall. Catch. Repeat. Do 8 reps.

Strengthening the glutes, hamstrings, quads, and calves can help cyclists unlock (and maintain) the muscular power and endurance needed to tackle hills, power through speed intervals, and resist fatigue on long rides. It can also improve your movement quality off the bike. “A comprehensive lower-body strength and mobility routine can help ensure muscle balance through the low back, hip, and knee, all necessary for maintaining appropriate gait and postural control,” Logue claims.

It has been revealed that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, a box, and a hex bar.

Stand inside the hex bar, feet hip-width apart, toes forward. (Or hold a dumbbell in each hand down in front of you.) Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core engaged, shoulders down and back. Lower torso toward floor until parallel or you feel a pull in hamstrings. Maintain a slight bend in knees. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending hips. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

According to recent reports, stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Hold a dumbbell vertically at chest with both hands. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

In a recent development, stand behind a step or box, holding a dumbbell in each hand, down by sides. Place right foot on top. Drive through right foot to stand up, extending knee and hips. Drive left knee up to hip height at top. Slowly lower back down. Step off box. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back, dumbbells framing foot. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted. Place one or two dumbbells on hips. Drive through feet to lift hips up, engaging glutes, hamstrings, and core. Avoid lifting with lower back. Slowly lower hips back down. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

In a recent development, if you want to capitalize on the benefits of strength training but only have time to train a couple of times a week, this full-body strength workout is the way to go. By incorporating compound movements, you’ll hit every major muscle group with just a handful of exercises.

Industry observers note that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps indicated, resting one minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and dumbbells.

It has been revealed that stand with feet hip-width apart. Lift right heel and line right toes up with left heel. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, down in front of you. This is the starting position. Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core tight. Lower torso toward floor, slight bend in knees, until you feel a pull in hamstrings or torso is parallel to floor. Drive through left foot to stand up, extending hips and returning to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders, elbows bent and palms facing each other. Send hips down and back to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending arms overhead as you stand. Return weights to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

According to recent reports, start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and hands on dumbbells, forming a straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows to lower body to floor for a push-up, maintaining one straight line with body. Press back up. Row right weight to hip, keeping elbow close to side. Place back down. Repeat on left side. That’s 1 rep. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

According to recent reports, stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward, and at the top, curl weights to shoulders, bending elbows. Extend weights back down by sides. Repeat lunge, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating, with biceps curl at the top of each lunge. Do 10 reps per side.

In a recent development, lie faceup, knees bent, feet planted on the floor. Hold a weight in each hand, then extend arms up, weights over shoulders. Drive through heels, engaging glutes to lift hips up toward the ceiling. Body should form a straight line from shoulders to knees. Pause for a few seconds. Then lower back down slowly, while keeping arms extended. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

10-Minute Slow Yoga Practice to Counter the Chaos

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yoga isn’t the answer to everything.
  • Industry observers note that the challenge here, especially when your default state has been “go go go,” is to slow down.
  • Your goal today is relaxation, so you might want to keep a supportive prop—such as like a bolster, pillow, or yoga block—close by.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yoga isn’t the answer to everything. But when life gets stressful, your mat is a safe place to land. Amid moments of stress and chaos, a gentle yoga flow made up of intentional movement can help still your racing mind, regulate your breathing, and encourage overall well-being. This practice blends elements of yin yoga and a generally pared-down approach that feels like a truly restful beat rather than another item on your to-do list.

Industry observers note that the challenge here, especially when your default state has been “go go go,” is to slow down. It’s almost like you’re retraining your body, and reminding yourself that it’s okay to do so.

Your goal today is relaxation, so you might want to keep a supportive prop—such as like a bolster, pillow, or yoga block—close by.

Industry observers note that begin in Rock Pose today, which is a variation of Child’s Pose. Sit back on your heels, with your toes untucked, and keep your legs close together. Hinge forward to round your upper body over your legs, placing your forehead on your mat or a block. Drape your arms by your sides, palms facing upward, so you create a rock-like shape.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Extend your arms forward and press up onto your hands and knees. With your next inhalation, lower your belly, lift your chin and chest, and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Exhale as you round your back and tuck your chin in Cat Pose.

Repeat Cat and Cow 3 times each, moving with the pace of your breath.

Lower yourself all the way down onto the front side of your body. Widen your feet toward the back corners of your mat. Your elbows will be just underneath your shoulders—or slightly forward if you’re dealing with lower back tension. Then lift your chest and press your palms and forearms into the mat in Sphinx Pose.

If you have a block, you can use it on its highest setting by angling it toward you and allowing your forehead to rest against the support.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Still lying down, stack your hands, elbows bent and pointing toward the edges of mat, and rest your forehead on the backs of your hands.

Recent findings suggest that start to slide your right knee out to the right side of the mat so it’s about in line with your hip in Half Frog. You want your right leg to have about a 90-degree angle so the inner thigh and calf are facing the floor. Keep resting your forehead on your hands or turn your head to one side.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

When you’re ready, repeat on the opposite side.

Recent findings suggest that from Half Frog Pose with your left knee bent, take a deep breath in. As you exhale, let your left leg extend long and straight behind you. Drape your arms by your sides, palms facing up. Turn your head and your gaze in either direction and let your shoulders round toward the ground. Simply be.

Stay here in a reverse variation of Savasana for 3-5 minutes or as long as you’d like.

#45552. What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March
